courses.title: Rockets and the rocket equation
courses.summary: Why rockets are mostly fuel: thrust, specific impulse, the Tsiolkovsky equation, staging and the delta-v needed for orbit, with code and number labs.
outcomes: Learners can apply Δv = Isp·g₀·ln(m₀/m_f)
Learners can explain why staging helps
Learners can compare propellants by Isp
Learners can estimate the Δv budget to low Earth orbit

scenes.text: Ishaan is amazed that a launch vehicle at lift-off is mostly propellant.
The rocket equation explains why.

steps.title: Equation
steps.body: Δv = Isp · g₀ · ln(m₀/m_f). Isp (seconds) measures engine efficiency; g₀ = 9.81 m/s²; m₀ full mass, m_f empty mass.

steps.title: Logarithm hurts
steps.body: Doubling the mass ratio adds only ln 2 × Isp·g₀ more Δv; that's why reaching orbit is so hard.

activity.prompt: Compute Δv (m/s, rounded) from Isp, m₀ and m_f.
activity.starter:
import math
isp, m0, mf = map(float, input().split())   # specific impulse (s), initial mass, final mass
g0 = 9.81
dv = 0  # TODO: Tsiolkovsky: Isp * g0 * ln(m0 / mf)
print(f"{dv:.0f}")
activity.solution:
import math
isp, m0, mf = map(float, input().split())
g0 = 9.81
dv = isp * g0 * math.log(m0 / mf)
print(f"{dv:.0f}")

scenes.text: A multi-stage rocket throws away empty tanks and engines.
Each stage starts lighter, so its mass ratio counts fully.

steps.title: Staging
steps.body: Total Δv = sum of each stage's Δv. Discarding dead mass beats a single giant stage.

steps.title: Propellants
steps.body:
- Solid: simple, high thrust, lower Isp (~250–280 s)
- Kerosene/LOX: ~300–350 s
- Liquid hydrogen/LOX (cryogenic): ~450 s in vacuum
ISRO's LVM3 uses solid strap-ons, a liquid core stage and a cryogenic upper stage.

steps.title: Thrust vs efficiency
steps.body: Lift-off needs high thrust; upper stages benefit most from high Isp.

activity.prompt: Two stages: stage 1 gives 3,200 m/s, stage 2 gives 6,100 m/s. Total Δv in m/s?

lessons.title: Lab: The Δv budget to orbit

scenes.text: Orbital speed at 400 km is about 7.7 km/s.
Yet rockets need roughly 9.3–10 km/s of Δv.

steps.title: Losses
steps.body: Gravity losses (fighting gravity while climbing) and aerodynamic drag add roughly 1.5–2 km/s. Launching eastward near the equator gains Earth's rotation (up to ~0.46 km/s).

steps.title: Budget
steps.body: 7.7 (orbit) + 1.5 (gravity) + 0.3 (drag) − 0.4 (rotation) ≈ 9.1 km/s.

steps.title: Sriharikota
steps.body: India's spaceport at Sriharikota is on the east coast, so rockets launch over the sea toward the east.

courses.summary: Circular orbital speed and period, Kepler's third law, geostationary and sun-synchronous orbits, escape velocity and transfer orbits, with code and number labs.

lessons.title: Lab: Speed and period of a circular orbit

scenes.text: Diya watches the International Space Station cross the sky in a few minutes.
It circles Earth roughly every 92 minutes.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: v = √(GM/r), T = 2πr/v, with GM_Earth = 3.986×10¹⁴ m³/s² and r = R_Earth + altitude (R ≈ 6,371 km).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using altitude instead of radius from Earth's centre; mixing km and m.

activity.prompt: Read an altitude in km and print circular orbital speed (m/s) and period (minutes).
activity.starter:
import math
GM, R = 3.986e14, 6371e3
h_km = float(input())
r = R + h_km * 1000
v = 0  # TODO: circular orbital speed sqrt(GM / r)
T = 1  # TODO: period = 2*pi*r / v
print(f"{v:.0f} m/s {T / 60:.1f} min")
activity.solution:
import math
GM, R = 3.986e14, 6371e3
h_km = float(input())
r = R + h_km * 1000
v = math.sqrt(GM / r)
T = 2 * math.pi * r / v
print(f"{v:.0f} m/s {T / 60:.1f} min")

scenes.text: A DTH dish points at one fixed spot in the sky.

steps.title: Orbits
steps.body:
- GEO: ~35,786 km altitude, period = one sidereal day, appears fixed (TV, weather, communications)
- MEO: navigation constellations like GPS (~20,200 km)
- LEO: imaging, internet constellations, space stations
- Sun-synchronous (SSO): near-polar LEO, crosses each latitude at the same local solar time (good for consistent lighting in images)

steps.title: Latency
steps.body: GEO round trip ≈ 2 × 35,786 km / c ≈ 0.24 s just to the satellite and back, noticeable on calls.

steps.title: NavIC
steps.body: India's regional navigation system (IRNSS/NavIC) uses satellites in geostationary and inclined geosynchronous orbits.

scenes.text: To reach the Moon you don't need full escape velocity, but you must raise your orbit a lot.
A Hohmann transfer uses two burns.

steps.title: Escape velocity
steps.body: v_esc = √(2GM/R) ≈ 11.2 km/s at Earth's surface, √2 times the circular speed at that radius.

steps.title: Hohmann transfer
steps.body: Burn 1 raises apoapsis to the target orbit; coast half an ellipse; burn 2 circularises. Efficient but slow.

steps.title: Chandrayaan approach
steps.body: ISRO's lunar missions raised their orbits step by step with engine burns at perigee before heading to the Moon, saving propellant.

lessons.title: Lab: Range and cost per km

scenes.text: Priya drives 40 km a day in Pune.
Compare cost per km with a petrol car.

steps.title: Energy
steps.body: Range ≈ usable kWh × 1000 / consumption (Wh/km). Cost/km = (Wh/km ÷ 1000) × price per kWh.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: 30 kWh, 150 Wh/km → 200 km. At ₹8/kWh → ₹1.20/km. A petrol car at 15 km/L and ₹100/L costs about ₹6.7/km.

steps.title: Real range
steps.body: AC use, speed, load and cold/hot weather reduce real-world range compared with rated figures.

activity.prompt: Read usable kWh, consumption (Wh/km) and price per kWh. Print range and cost per km.
activity.starter:

scenes.text: A pack is hundreds of cells in series and parallel, plus a battery management system (BMS).
Series adds voltage; parallel adds capacity.

steps.title: Arithmetic
steps.body: Pack voltage = cells in series × cell voltage. Pack energy = voltage × amp-hours (Ah) of each parallel group.

steps.title: 96s3p of 3.6 V, 5 Ah cells
steps.body: Voltage ≈ 96 × 3.6 = 345.6 V. Capacity = 3 × 5 = 15 Ah. Energy ≈ 345.6 × 15 ≈ 5.18 kWh.

steps.title: BMS
steps.body: Monitors each cell's voltage and temperature, balances cells, limits current, and cuts off on faults.

steps.title: Comparison (general)
steps.body:
- NMC: higher energy density (more range per kg), uses nickel/cobalt, more sensitive to thermal runaway
- LFP: lower energy density, cheaper, very long cycle life, more thermally stable, cobalt-free

steps.title: Charging time
steps.body: Charging 24 kWh (e.g. 20→80% of 40 kWh) at 50 kW DC ≈ 0.48 h ≈ 29 min (real chargers taper near full).

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Damaged, overcharged or overheated lithium cells can enter thermal runaway. Use certified chargers; never charge swollen batteries (also true for e-bikes and phones).

steps.title: Recycling
steps.body: Recovering lithium, nickel, cobalt and copper reduces mining needs; second-life packs can serve as stationary storage.

scenes.text: A village cooperative wants a ledger nobody can quietly edit.
Step one: a hash, a short fingerprint of any data.

steps.title: Hash functions
steps.body: SHA-256 turns any input into 256 bits (64 hex characters). Same input → same output; tiny change → completely different output; infeasible to reverse or find collisions.

steps.title: Test vector
steps.body: sha256('abc') = ba7816bf…20015ad. Try 'Hello' vs 'hello': totally different digests.

steps.title: Not encryption
steps.body: A hash can't be 'decrypted'. Short or guessable inputs (like phone numbers) can be brute-forced, so hashing alone doesn't anonymise.

lessons.title: Lab: Link blocks into a chain

story.title: Why history is hard to rewrite

scenes.text: Each block stores the previous block's hash.
Edit block 1 and every later hash changes.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Block = (previous hash, data, timestamp, nonce). The chain's latest hash depends on every earlier block.

steps.title: Tamper test
steps.body: Change 'pays Ravi 5' to 'pays Ravi 50' → the final hash changes, so anyone holding the true tip detects the edit.

steps.title: What makes it secure
steps.body: Linking only detects tampering. Preventing a rewrite needs many independent copies plus a consensus rule (proof of work or stake).

activity.prompt: Build a 3-block toy chain (8-char hashes), print the tip, then show that tampering changes it.
activity.hint: prev = H(prev + data)[:8] inside each loop

options: Publicly replicated on many nodes (for public chains)

scenes.text: Miners search for a nonce so the block hash starts with zeros.
Each extra hex zero means ~16× more work on average.

steps.title: Difficulty
steps.body: Requiring k leading hex zeros means a 1 in 16ᵏ chance per try. '00' ≈ 256 tries on average; '000' ≈ 4,096.

steps.title: Our toy
steps.body: For prefix 'block-42:', the first nonce giving a hash starting '00' is 273.

steps.title: Bitcoin
steps.body: The network adjusts difficulty so a block is found about every 10 minutes (~144 per day). This consumes large amounts of electricity, a real cost of proof of work.

activity.prompt: Find the first nonce n such that sha256('block-42:' + n) starts with '00'. Print n and the first 6 hex characters.
activity.starter:

lessons.title: The shell, the prompt and command anatomy

scenes.text: Arjun joins a hosting company in Pune. His lead gives him a login to dev01.contoso.local.
He sees [arjun@dev01 ~]$ and a blinking cursor. Where is he, who is he, and what can he type?

steps.title: What a shell is
steps.body:
The **shell** (usually **bash**) is a program that reads a line you type, expands it (variables, wildcards, quotes) and starts other programs.

- `[arjun@dev01 ~]$` = user **arjun**, host **dev01**, current directory **~** (home), `$` = normal user (`#` = root).
- Command anatomy: `command -options arguments`, e.g. `ls -l /etc`.
- Short options combine: `ls -la` = `ls -l -a`. Long options use two dashes: `ls --all`.

steps.title: Solved example: reading a command
steps.body:
`cp -rv /etc/nginx /root/nginx-backup`

- `cp` = command (copy)
- `-r` = recursive (directories), `-v` = verbose
- `/etc/nginx` = source, `/root/nginx-backup` = destination.

Second example: `tail -n 20 /var/log/messages` prints the last 20 lines of the system log.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Linux is **case-sensitive**: `Documents` ≠ `documents`.
- Spaces separate arguments: `cd My Files` tries to go to `My`. Quote it: `cd "My Files"`.
- Do not work as root for everyday tasks; use `sudo` only when needed.

quiz.why: By convention root's prompt ends in #, normal users' in $.

quiz.q: How do you cd into a directory named `My Files`?

scenes.text: Arjun's lead asks: 'Find the nginx config and the nginx logs, then come back home.'

steps.title: The FHS map
steps.body:
- `/` root of everything (one tree, even with many disks)
- `/etc` system configuration (text files)
- `/var` variable data: `/var/log` logs, `/var/lib` databases, `/var/spool` queues
- `/home` users' homes; `/root` root's home
- `/usr` installed programs and libraries (`/usr/bin`, `/usr/lib`)
- `/tmp` temporary files (often cleaned at boot)
- `/proc`, `/sys` virtual files exposing kernel state
- `/dev` device files (`/dev/sda`, `/dev/null`)
- `/boot` kernel and bootloader files

steps.title: Absolute vs relative paths
steps.body:
Absolute starts at `/`: `/var/log/nginx`.
Relative starts where you are: if you are in `/var`, then `log/nginx` is the same place.

- `.` = current dir, `..` = parent, `~` = home, `cd -` = previous dir.

Example: from `/etc/nginx/conf.d`, `cd ../..` lands in `/etc`.

steps.title: Always check where you are
steps.body: `pwd` prints the working directory. Run it before any `rm`.

steps.title: Core file commands
steps.body:

- `touch f` creates an empty file or updates its timestamp

- `mv old new` renames or moves

`cp notes.txt{,.bak}` expands to `cp notes.txt notes.txt.bak` — a quick backup.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `rm -rf / tmp/x` (stray space) is catastrophic. Read the line twice.
- `mv a b` silently overwrites `b`; use `mv -i` or `-n`.
- `cp dir dst` without `-r` fails: 'omitting directory'.

lessons.title: Lab: Links, inodes, globbing and find

scenes.text: Two files show the same content and editing one changes the other. A colleague says: 'It's a hard link.'

steps.title: Inodes and links
steps.body:
Each file's metadata (owner, mode, size, block pointers) lives in an **inode**; a directory entry maps a name to an inode number (`ls -i`).

- **Hard link** `ln a b`: a second name for the same inode; same filesystem only; file survives until the last link is removed.
- **Symbolic link** `ln -s target name`: a small file containing a path; can cross filesystems; breaks if the target moves.

steps.title: Globbing and find
steps.body:
Globs are expanded by the shell: `*.log`, `file?.txt`, `[abc]*`.

`find /var -name '*.log' -size +100M` — files over 100 MiB.
`find /tmp -type f -mtime +7 -delete` — delete files modified more than 7 days ago.
`find / -user arjun 2>/dev/null` — files owned by arjun, errors hidden.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Quote patterns for find (`-name '*.log'`) or the shell expands them first.
- Test `find … -print` before adding `-delete`.

steps.title: Three standard streams
steps.body:
- 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr
- `>` overwrite stdout to file, `>>` append
- `2>` stderr, `&>` or `>file 2>&1` both
- `<` feed a file as stdin
- `|` connects stdout of one command to stdin of the next
- `tee file` writes to a file AND passes data on

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. `backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1` — append both streams.
2. `dnf list installed | wc -l` — count installed package lines.
3. `df -h | tee /tmp/df.txt` — see output and save it.

steps.title: Order matters
steps.body: `cmd 2>&1 > file` sends stderr to the *terminal* (where stdout pointed at that moment) and only stdout to file. Write `cmd > file 2>&1`.

steps.title: grep essentials
steps.body:
- `grep -i` ignore case, `-v` invert, `-n` line numbers, `-c` count, `-r` recursive, `-l` file names only
- `-E` extended regex: `+ ? | ()` without backslashes
- `-o` print only the matching part
- Anchors `^` start, `$` end; `.` any char; `[0-9]` class; `{1,3}` repetition

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
`grep 'Failed password' /var/log/secure | grep -oE '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`

Result: a ranked list of attacking IPs. Second example: `grep -v '^#' /etc/ssh/sshd_config | grep -v '^$'` shows only active settings.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `-E` so `+` is literal in basic regex.
- `grep error` misses `ERROR`; use `-i`.

lessons.title: Reading ls -l and the rwx model

scenes.text: Kavya in Finance says she can see report.xlsx on the share but 'Permission denied' when opening it.

steps.title: Ten characters
steps.body:
`-rw-r----- 1 ravi finance 8192 Nov 26 report.xlsx`

- 1st char: type (`-` file, `d` dir, `l` link)
- Then three triplets: **user (owner)**, **group**, **others**
- r=4, w=2, x=1 → rw-r----- = **640**

steps.title: On directories it's different
steps.body:
- **r** list names
- **w** create, delete, rename entries (needs x too)
- **x** enter/traverse (`cd`, access files inside)

So deleting a file depends on the *directory's* w, not the file's.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. `rwxr-x---` = 7,5,0 = **750**.
2. 644 = rw-r--r--: owner edits, everyone reads.
3. Kavya is not ravi and not in group finance → 'others' = --- → denied.

- `chmod -R u=rwX,g=rX,o= /srv/app` — capital X: execute only on directories (or already-executable files)

steps.title: umask
steps.body:
New files start from 666, directories from 777; the umask bits are **removed**.

- umask 022 → files 644, dirs 755
- umask 027 → files 640, dirs 750
- umask 077 → files 600, dirs 700

Set per shell with `umask 027`, per systemd service with `UMask=0027`.

steps.title: setuid, setgid, sticky
steps.body:
- **setuid (4)** on an executable: runs as file owner (`/usr/bin/passwd` → `-rwsr-xr-x`)
- **setgid (2)** on a directory: new files inherit the directory's group
- **sticky (1)** on a directory: only owner can delete their files (`/tmp` → `drwxrwxrwt`)

`chmod 2770 /srv/shared` = setgid + rwxrwx---.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: umask 027, new dir: 777 − 027 → 750. New file: 666 with 027 masked → 640 (umask removes bits; it is not plain subtraction, e.g. 666 with umask 033 → 644).

- `setfacl -d -m u:audit1:rX /srv/finance` **default** ACL for future files
- `getfacl /srv/finance` view; `setfacl -x u:audit1` remove one; `setfacl -b` remove all
- `ls -l` shows a `+` after the mode when an ACL exists

steps.title: The mask
steps.body: The ACL **mask** caps group-class entries (named users, named groups, owning group). If mask is `r--`, a named user given `rwx` is effectively `r--`. chmod on the group bits changes the mask.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the default ACL so new files are invisible to the auditor.
- Copying with tools that don't preserve ACLs (use `cp -a`, `rsync -A`).

steps.title: Tools

scenes.text: Half the outages last month were 'just DNS'.
Nikhita maps the full path.

steps.title: Flow
steps.body: App → stub resolver (glibc, nsswitch) → configured resolver (e.g. 10.20.0.10 or systemd-resolved 127.0.0.53) → recursive lookup: root → TLD (.local is special; use real zones in production) → authoritative server → answer cached for TTL

steps.title: Records
steps.body:
- A / AAAA: IPv4 / IPv6
- CNAME: alias
- MX: mail servers (priority)
- TXT: SPF, verification
- NS: delegation; SOA: zone metadata (serial, refresh, negative TTL)
- PTR: reverse lookup

steps.title: TTL
steps.body: TTL 3600 → resolvers may serve the old IP for up to an hour after a change. Lower it days before migrations.

steps.title: Pieces

lessons.title: The USE method and load average

scenes.text: Three vague tickets a day say 'slow'. Senior admin Vikas teaches a method.
Utilisation, Saturation, Errors — for every resource.

steps.title: USE
steps.body:
For each resource (CPU, memory, disk, network):
- **Utilisation** — how busy (CPU %, disk %util)
- **Saturation** — queued work (run queue, swap activity, disk queue/await)
- **Errors** — (dmesg, NIC errors, disk errors)

steps.title: Load average
steps.body:
1/5/15-minute averages of tasks **running or waiting for CPU, plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (D)** on Linux.

Compare to CPU count (`nproc`): load 4 on 8 CPUs ≈ 50% demand; load 16 on 8 ≈ saturated. High load with idle CPU → likely I/O (D state).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `uptime` → load 12.3, 11.8, 6.1 on 4 CPUs: saturation started ~10 min ago and is rising (1-min > 15-min).

bands.text: Busy: close to full CPU demand.
Saturated: tasks are queueing. Check whether they're R (CPU) or D (I/O).
Severe saturation: expect latency; act now (find culprit, shed load).

quiz.why: Correct answer: Runnable tasks and D-state (uninterruptible) tasks.
Correct answer: About 3× more demand than CPUs.
Correct answer: Load is rising recently.

scenes.text: app16 slow; top shows 100% CPU.

steps.title: CPU breakdown
steps.body:
top header `%Cpu(s): us sy ni id wa hi si st`:
- **us** user code, **sy** kernel, **wa** waiting on I/O (CPU idle!), **st** stolen by hypervisor (noisy neighbour)
- `vmstat 1 5`: **r** run queue, **b** blocked (D), **si/so** swap in/out, **wa**
- In top: `1` per-CPU, `P` sort CPU, `M` sort memory, `H` threads

steps.title: Readings
steps.body:
- us 92% → app code busy (profile/scale)
- sy 40% → syscalls/contention
- wa 60% → disks slow
- st 25% → VM starved: talk to virtualisation team

steps.title: Per-process

scenes.text: Devs ship everything as containers; ops must run them.

steps.title: Kernel features
steps.body:
- **Namespaces** isolate views: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user
- **cgroups** limit/account CPU, memory, I/O
- **Image**: layered read-only filesystem (OCI format) + a thin writable layer
- Container = process(es) with those settings; shares the host kernel
- VM = full guest kernel on a hypervisor

steps.title: See it
steps.body: `podman run -d --name web nginx` → `ps -ef | grep nginx` on the host shows the processes; `lsns` lists namespaces.

steps.title: Podman vs Docker
steps.body: Podman is daemonless and rootless-friendly (default on RHEL); CLI is largely Docker-compatible (`alias docker=podman`).

- Bind mount: `-v /srv/site:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro,Z`
- **:Z** relabels for this container only (private), **:z** shared between containers (SELinux hosts)
- Rootless: run as normal user; ports < 1024 need extra config; storage under `~/.local/share/containers`

steps.body: Bind mount without :Z on an SELinux host → app gets 'Permission denied' reading files. Add `:Z` (never on system dirs like /home or /usr).
